title: Pitchei Teshuva on Shulchan Arukh, Even HaEzer
heTitle: פתחי תשובה על שולחן ערוך אבן העזר

text: Double condition: The Avnei HaEzer, in the name of the Beit Shmuel, writes that this means the condition must be stated at the time of intercourse. However, one who examines the Beit Shmuel will see that this matter is not clear to him, and he questions this, since it can be argued that there is no need to stipulate at the time of intercourse, as here we can say that it is not an act of promiscuity at all. See on this topic the responsum of Noda BiYehuda, section 54, which will be cited shortly.However, in the responsa I referenced in the previous subsection, their view is explained that one must repeat and stipulate before two proper witnesses before the first intercourse, and say before them that upon this condition shall be all his acts of intercourse. In the responsum of Rabbi Akiva Eiger, he added that he should take an oath before witnesses that he will not betroth her afterward and will never nullify these conditions, so that there will be no concern regarding the other acts of intercourse, for even if he nullifies the condition, since he swore before witnesses, we can say that if he does so it is ineffective. And what the Avnei HaEzer writes in the name of the Noda BiYehuda, that the same applies when there is a deaf brother—and the Shvut Yaakov disagrees with him. See in the aforementioned responsa that their view is like the Noda BiYehuda, that even with a deaf brother, or when the brother has been missing for several years and his location is unknown, one may betroth conditionally. And in the responsum of Chatam Sofer there, he writes that he received this lenient ruling from his teachers and indeed performed such an act with someone who had a missing brother.And there in the responsum of Noda BiYehuda section 54, he was asked about a case of a woman whose husband died without children, and there remained a deaf brother, and the woman says that when she was betrothed to her husband, there was a condition in the betrothal that if her husband dies without children, the betrothal would be retroactively void. The one who arranged these betrothals was Rabbi Yuzpa of blessed memory. She also said that the rabbi commanded her to say this with every act of intercourse. The witnesses who were at the time of the betrothal had already passed away. After they announced that whoever has any knowledge should come testify, two judges of the community came and testified that they heard from the rabbi after the wedding that the betrothal was conditional. Then one witness came who saw in the rabbi's estate among his writings a form on paper that this woman was betrothed conditionally. Then a second witness testified that he was present at the wedding and heard how the rabbi arranged the betrothal word by word in the manner of the aforementioned condition. He was asked whether there is substance to the aforementioned testimony, since the testimony of the two judges is considered hearsay, and the testimony of the first witness who saw a form in the rabbi's handwriting also doesn't count as testimony, for even if we had the rabbi's handwriting before us, it would be one witness in a document and would not be effective. Only the testimony of the second witness remains, and he is only one witness. He responded at length, and the essence of his words is that it is clear that releasing a yevama to the marketplace is not called a matter of sexual prohibition, for it is neither subject to death penalty nor to karet, only to a negative commandment. In matters that are not sexual prohibitions and where there is no established prohibition, certainly one witness is believed. And even if the prohibition was established and it is in his hand, he is believed, as with slaughter where the prohibition was established and the slaughterer is believed, and a menstruant woman is believed to say she immersed. But when it is not in his hand, the Tosafot write that we are uncertain about this. However, there is room to rule leniently in our case, for from the words of Maimonides it is explained that regarding a man and woman, even though they conduct themselves with the presumption of marriage, this is still not called an established fact that she is his wife absolutely without condition, until they say explicitly "this is my wife" and "this is my husband." Therefore, one who says there was a condition in the betrothal is not testifying against an established presumption. Furthermore, immediately after the wedding ceremony, it cannot be said that she has been established as requiring levirate marriage. If at that time one witness testified that she was betrothed conditionally, it certainly would be effective. And specifically regarding a condition that depends on after his death, which is not testifying about a matter of sexual prohibition, since all his lifetime we have no concern with the condition. Since the two judges of the community testify that the rabbi said immediately after the wedding that she was betrothed conditionally, we have two witnesses that the rabbi testified at a time when his testimony was effective. Additionally, there is permission in our case since it was his custom in all such situations to betroth conditionally for the benefit of the woman, and it has been clarified to us that the rabbi who arranged the betrothal intended to betroth in this manner. Therefore, since it is a customary matter, the testimony of the second witness who testifies that he was present at the wedding and heard that the rabbi arranged the betrothal on this condition is effective. For where something is customary, one witness is believed even in matters of sexual prohibition, even if a prohibition has been established. However, the difficulty is that all these witnesses are about the wedding and betrothal, but there is no witness about the seclusion and intercourse. Nevertheless, it appears that if she says with certainty that there was a condition also at the time of intercourse, she is believed. And even though there is a presumption that a person does not engage in promiscuous relations, meaning he has intercourse without specification intending for betrothal, this is only when both he and she are silent. But if she is not willing to have intercourse with him except conditionally, there is no presumption here, and therefore she is believed to say that she had intercourse explicitly on this condition.
